notes.meaning: Early in the morning, the Jewish leaders gathered to finalize their charges against Jesus, then tied Him up and took Him to Pontius Pilate. Roman officials normally began holding court at dawn, so the leaders acted right away. Under Roman rule, the Jewish council lacked the authority to carry out an execution, so they had to seek a death sentence from the Roman governor.

Pilate asked Jesus directly whether He was the King of the Jews, and Jesus answered, 'You have said so.' A claim to royalty was the only charge Pilate cared about, because setting up a rival kingdom was treason against Rome. Jesus agreed that He is indeed the King, though His kingdom was not the political threat the religious leaders claimed.

The chief priests poured out many accusations against Jesus before the governor. They tried hard to paint Him as a dangerous troublemaker and rebel. Through all their harsh charges, Jesus stayed calm and did not trade insults with them.

Pilate questioned Jesus again, asking why He made no effort to answer such serious charges. Roman legal hearings expected an accused person to put up a strong self-defense. Pilate was surprised that a man on trial for His life would remain silent.

Jesus gave no further answer, leaving Pilate completely amazed. His silence was not guilt, but quiet dignity and complete trust in God's plan. This fulfilled ancient prophecy that God's servant would suffer without opening His mouth.

It was the governor's regular practice to release one prisoner to the people during the Passover festival. The crowd was allowed to choose whoever they wanted set free. This holiday pardon gave Pilate a possible opening to let Jesus go.

A prisoner named Barabbas was locked up alongside rebels who had committed murder during a violent uprising. While Jesus was falsely accused of treason, Barabbas was an actual terrorist and killer against the Roman peace. He faced certain death for his crimes.

The crowd came forward and asked Pilate to grant them the usual holiday pardon. They wanted him to keep his regular custom of freeing a prisoner. This gave the governor a chance to test what the people thought of Jesus.

Pilate asked the crowd whether they wanted him to release 'the King of the Jews.' He hoped the ordinary people would choose Jesus instead of a notorious criminal. Using that royal title also reminded them how shameful it would be to demand the death of their own king.

Pilate could see clearly that the chief priests brought Jesus to him out of jealousy. They were envious of His popularity, teachings, and miracles, not concerned with real Roman law. The governor knew the charges against Jesus were dishonest.

The chief priests stirred up the crowd to demand the release of Barabbas instead of Jesus. They worked through the people, talking them into choosing a violent criminal over the peaceful healer. The mob gave in to the pressure of their leaders.

Pilate asked the crowd again what they wanted him to do with the man they called King of the Jews. He was shocked that they would let a murderer go and leave Jesus in chains. He forced them to state plainly what fate they had in mind for Him.

The crowd yelled back with one voice, demanding that Jesus be crucified. Crucifixion was the most painful, shameful death sentence known in the Roman world. Nothing less than the complete destruction of Jesus would satisfy them.

Pilate pressed them for reasons, asking what evil Jesus had actually done. He openly judged Jesus to be innocent of any crime worthy of death. Instead of offering evidence, the crowd simply shouted louder and louder for Him to be crucified.

Pilate chose to satisfy the noisy crowd to protect his own position, so he released Barabbas. He ordered Jesus to be flogged with leather whips tipped with bone or metal, and then handed Him over to be crucified. In this swap, the guilty rebel walked away free while the innocent Savior took his place.

The soldiers took Jesus into the palace courtyard, called the Praetorium, and called together the whole company on duty. This was the governor's headquarters where Roman troops stayed. They gathered around the wounded prisoner to make fun of Him.

The soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe and placed a crown made of twisted thorns onto His head. Purple was the color of kings, so they put an old soldier's cloak on Him as a mock royal outfit. The sharp thorns formed a painful, mocking crown that cut into His skin.

They shouted out to Him, 'Hail, King of the Jews!' This twisted the formal greeting used to honor the Roman emperor, turning it into cruel ridicule. They treated the true King of creation like a worthless joke.

The soldiers repeatedly hit Jesus on the head with a wooden staff, spat on Him, and fell on their knees in fake worship. Hitting Him drove the sharp thorns deeper into His temples. Their pretend reverence was meant to heap total humiliation upon His bodily pain.

When they finished their cruel game, the soldiers stripped the purple robe off Jesus and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they led Him out of the city gates toward the execution hill. Every step He took brought Him closer to the cross.

As they marched, the soldiers forced Simon from Cyrene in North Africa to carry the heavy crossbeam for Jesus. Jesus' strength had failed after the terrible beating He received. Mark identifies Simon as the father of Alexander and Rufus, two men well known to the early church.

They brought Jesus to a location called Golgotha, which means 'The Place of the Skull.' This public execution site lay just outside the walls of Jerusalem. It was a grim place where many condemned men had died.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: An ancient church tradition holds that Golgotha was the burial place of Adam, which is why Eastern Orthodox icons regularly depict Adam's skull beneath the feet of the crucified Christ.

notes.meaning: They offered Jesus wine mixed with myrrh, a drugged drink used to dull pain, but He refused it. He chose to remain fully clear-minded so He could feel the full weight of the cross. He would not avoid any part of the suffering His Father had set before Him.

The soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross and raised Him up to die. They divided His clothes among themselves, casting lots to see what each soldier would take. While He hung in agony, this casual gambling fulfilled the exact words of Psalm 22.
